Day 42 of 100 · Linux Administration

Linux Permissions

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

Permissions and ownership determine which users and groups can read, modify or execute files and directories.

Architecture / mental model

user identity + group membership → owner/group/other mode bits → allowed filesystem operation

How it works

Traditional Unix permissions apply read, write and execute bits separately to owner, group and others. On directories, those bits have directory-specific meaning: execute controls traversal, read controls listing and write controls entry creation/removal when other conditions allow it.

Ownership is as important as numeric modes. A configuration file with `600` is not safe if it is owned by the wrong account, and recursively changing ownership can break services that rely on specific identities.

Special modes such as setuid, setgid and the sticky bit exist for particular use cases and deserve deliberate review because they change normal permission behavior.

Hands-on reference

ls -l PATH
stat PATH
chmod 640 file
chown root:app file

Verification

Check both `ls -l` and `stat`, then test access using the actual service or user identity rather than assuming the mode string tells the whole story.

Field note / gotcha

Directory write permission can allow deleting a file even when the file itself is not writable, because deletion changes the directory entry.

Security considerations

Avoid world-writable files and careless recursive chmod/chown. Apply the minimum access required to the exact path.

What I learned

Permissions are an access-control model, not a collection of magic numbers to copy from Stack Overflow.
